decisions.question: OQ-N2: Do routes carry typed arguments (Route<Args>) or untyped maps?

options.label: typed NavRoute<A>, arguments optional A?
options.consequence: compile-time checking of an intent's arguments against its route; RouteState equality and nav.current-route dedup work through the app's value types; deep-link resolvers and redirects build typed arguments; arguments are not required at the call, as the Guide's are not

options.label: untyped Map<String, Object?> arguments
options.consequence: the Guide §3.2 sketch; no checking; Dart maps have no value equality, so equal RouteStates compare unequal and the topic's default dedup never fires; destinations cast

options.label: typed and required arguments, separate classes for routes with and without arguments
options.consequence: presence is checked too, at the cost of two route types and the registry complexity Guide §3.2 warns about

decisions.chosen: typed NavRoute<A>, arguments optional A?
decisions.why: Owner's standing preference for types and ADTs, Spec §4.2's compile-time typing for topics as the analogue, and a Dart-specific reason the Guide does not weigh: map arguments break RouteState equality (Spec §3.12 dedup is Dart ==). Guide §3.6's own example already passes a typed request as args. Optional rather than required because deep links and platform routes can arrive without arguments. Signal that would change it: an app whose routes are all argument-free, or one generated from routes.yaml where codegen could make presence checkable cheaply.

decisions.question: How are GoTo, Replace and ShowModal built so that their arguments are checked against the route?

options.label: built only by route methods (route.go(args)), no public constructor
options.consequence: the receiver fixes A, so a wrong argument is argument_type_not_assignable; reads route-first rather than as the Guide's constructor

options.label: public generic constructors GoTo<A>(route, args)
options.consequence: the Guide's spelling, but Dart infers A from both arguments and widens it, so GoTo(order, 'seven') compiles

decisions.chosen: built only by route methods (route.go(args)), no public constructor
decisions.why: The probe shows the generic constructor widens (W6 compiles; W6b with a typed context does not), the same inference topology-dsl@v1 G3 had to work around. Back, BackTo, DismissModal and DeepLink keep public const constructors because they carry no arguments.

decisions.question: OQ-N1: How does the library's resolver template bind to an app's own auth state type, which Guide §3.4's resolver reads directly?

options.label: generic template over the app's auth StateTopic<S> with a pure projection to a library AccessPrincipal
options.consequence: the resolver reads the app's auth topic directly as Guide §3.4 and Appendix A draw; one pure guard over library types; apps with richer guards project facts into roles or a CustomAccess test, or write their own resolver from the public pure functions

options.label: template takes a guard function and the topics it reads
options.consequence: maximum flexibility, but the topology DSL's withLatestFrom arities fix how many topics a guard can read, the template becomes a thin wrapper, and applyAuthGuard is only a default

options.label: a library topic nav.access-principal the app writes from its auth state
options.consequence: no generic template, but a sixth navigation topic the node spec and Guide §3.3 do not list, and one more state topic with an owner the app must provide

decisions.chosen: generic template over the app's auth StateTopic<S> with a pure projection to a library AccessPrincipal
decisions.why: It keeps the Guide's graph (nav-resolver reads auth.state), keeps the app's auth type the app's, and keeps the guard a pure function, which the owner's functional-first preference favors. The other two remain open to an app because every piece of the template is public. Signal that would change it: a v1 app whose guard needs several app topics that cannot be combined into one state topic.

decisions.question: What does the guard do while the app's auth state is still initializing at a cold-start deep link?

options.label: a PendingPrincipal variant with its own redirect, defaulting to the unauthenticated one
options.consequence: a three-state principal; the app can send a protected cold-start deep link to a splash that waits, rather than flashing login

options.label: two-state principal, the projection maps initializing to anonymous
options.consequence: simpler; every authenticated cold-start deep link to a protected route goes through login first

options.label: hold intents in the resolver until auth is known
options.consequence: needs a buffering stage the topology DSL expresses only through switchMap or rawEngine; switchMap would cancel queued intents

decisions.chosen: a PendingPrincipal variant with its own redirect, defaulting to the unauthenticated one
decisions.why: Spec §7.6's Initializing variant and Guide §3.5's cold-start deep link meet exactly at the guard; a guard that cannot tell not-yet-known from signed-out forces a login flash. Holding is deferred (Versioning) because the DSL has no safe buffering combinator. Signal: an app that wants holding semantics in the library.

decisions.question: Where does a refused intent go, given that a library guard cannot name the app's login and unauthorized routes (Guide §3.4 hardcodes AuthRoutes.login with a returnTo map)?

options.label: AccessRedirects: app-provided pure functions from the attempted intent to the intent to perform
options.consequence: typed, so a login route can carry the attempted intent as its argument; the redirect's result is not guarded again

options.label: the policy carries redirect routes and the guard builds GoTo(route, returnTo)
options.consequence: less app code, but fixes the redirect's argument shape and puts functions or routes into a state-topic value

decisions.chosen: AccessRedirects: app-provided pure functions from the attempted intent to the intent to perform
decisions.why: Keeps RouteAccessPolicy the Spec Appendix A.6 map from route to requirement and lets the app type its redirect arguments. No evidence beyond the typing argument.

decisions.question: In which order does the resolver guard and resolve deep links?

options.label: resolve first, then guard the resolved intent
options.consequence: a deep link to a protected route is guarded; applyAuthGuard takes and returns ResolvedNavIntent

options.label: guard first, then resolve, as Guide §3.4 writes
options.consequence: a DeepLink has no target route before resolution, passes the guard, and its resolved target is never checked: a guard bypass

decisions.chosen: resolve first, then guard the resolved intent
decisions.why: The Guide's order lets any deep link bypass the auth guard; the conformance case G14 'resolves a deep link before it guards it' and the executor case G24 'guarded after it is resolved' pin the fix on both platforms.

decisions.question: How is ResolvedNavIntent declared so that a deep link is impossible by construction?

options.label: a sealed subfamily of NavIntent: NavIntent = DeepLink | ResolvedNavIntent
options.consequence: six variants declared once; resolveDeepLinks passes resolved intents through; a resolved intent can be published to nav.intent

options.label: two parallel sealed families, as Guide §3.2 sketches
options.consequence: each variant declared twice and mapped one by one in resolveDeepLinks

decisions.chosen: a sealed subfamily of NavIntent: NavIntent = DeepLink | ResolvedNavIntent
decisions.why: Spec Appendix A.6 defines the resolved type as identical to NavIntent except DeepLink, which a subfamily states exactly; topic-model@v1's MultiWriterTopic is the precedent in this tree. Reject codes confirmed against the stand-in.

decisions.question: The Specification and the Guide name the route type Route, which package:flutter/widgets.dart also exports. Keep the name or rename it?

options.label: NavRoute
options.consequence: no collision in Flutter pages; consistent with NavIntent; deviates from the glossary name

options.label: Route, with apps hiding Flutter's
options.consequence: the glossary name; every Flutter file importing both libraries writes hide Route or a prefix, or gets ambiguous_import

decisions.chosen: NavRoute
decisions.why: The probe shows ambiguous_import on Route and no collision for any other navigation-api name with package:flutter/material.dart. Every page that publishes intents also builds widgets. nidana.navigation's Owns list says Route; the contract's name is the binding one.

decisions.question: What does the executor protocol consist of, and what does a platform implement?

options.label: a final NavigationExecutor in this package over a NavigationRouter port the platform implements
options.consequence: claim, observe, planning, BackTo synthesis, paired writes, timestamps, diagnostics and disposal written once; a platform implements four stack calls, its stack and its confirmations; flutter-binding@v1's FlutterNavigationExecutor is a Flutter router with wiring, not a subclass

options.label: an abstract base executor each platform subclasses
options.consequence: the Guide's FlutterNavigationExecutor-is-a-NavigationExecutor shape; template-method inheritance the owner's composition preference disfavors

options.label: an interface only; each platform writes the whole executor
options.consequence: Guide §3.4 literally; every platform reimplements the bus logic, and the suite tests each copy

decisions.chosen: a final NavigationExecutor in this package over a NavigationRouter port the platform implements
decisions.why: nidana.navigation's spec already owns the bus-facing duties (claim, paired writes, BackTo synthesis) and nidana.flutter's spec owns only the implementation against its router, so the split follows the node specs; composition over inheritance per the owner. Node set and contract set unchanged, so not a tree-shape stop.

decisions.question: What does each intent do to the stack (the Specification is silent; Guide §3.4 maps GoTo to go_router's location-based go)?

options.label: GoTo pushes; Replace replaces the top; Back pops; BackTo pops to the topmost entry of its route; ShowModal pushes modal; DismissModal pops a modal
options.consequence: one meaning every router can realize, so one suite checks every platform; BackTo and Replace stay distinct; no reset-the-stack intent in v1; flutter-binding must map GoTo to push

options.label: GoTo resets the stack to the route (go semantics)
options.consequence: matches the Guide's go_router mapping on flat routes; stack contents depend on the router's route tree; Back after GoTo is usually at the root, which leaves BackTo nearly useless

decisions.chosen: GoTo pushes; Replace replaces the top; Back pops; BackTo pops to the topmost entry of its route; ShowModal pushes modal; DismissModal pops a modal
decisions.why: A portable conformance suite needs one stack meaning, and BackTo's presence in the vocabulary implies stacks grown by GoTo. Close call against go semantics; the signal that would change it is an owner preference for URL-location navigation on web, which would add a reset intent rather than redefine GoTo.

decisions.question: What does the executor do with an intent the stack does not admit (Back at the root, BackTo a route not on the stack, DismissModal with no modal on top)?

options.label: refuse: nothing navigates or is written; dev mode reports NavigationRefused
options.consequence: uniform across routers; a Flutter pop of the last route cannot happen through intents

options.label: pass the call to the platform
options.consequence: router-defined results, such as an empty Navigator

decisions.chosen: refuse: nothing navigates or is written; dev mode reports NavigationRefused
decisions.why: Keeps behavior the same on every router and the suite router-neutral; uses bus-api@v1's ShellDiagnostic extension point (root D8). The diagnostic holds the reason and BackTo's route, never arguments (bus-api@v1 G4). BackTo to the route already on top is a no-op, not a refusal.

decisions.question: How does a router report transitions, and how many history entries does a synthesized BackTo produce?

options.label: one perform per intent, validated before acting, confirmed once with the stack it left and the intent; platform transitions confirmed with const Back()
options.consequence: a synthesized BackTo (k pops) and a native popUntil both yield one transition; routers must suppress their own observer events during a perform

options.label: one confirmation per platform pop
options.consequence: a synthesized BackTo writes k transitions and a native popUntil also k (Flutter observers see each pop), so history differs from the intent stream

decisions.chosen: one perform per intent, validated before acting, confirmed once with the stack it left and the intent; platform transitions confirmed with const Back()
decisions.why: Guide §3.4 requires history and currentRoute to agree and the intent to come from the platform's confirmation; one transition per intent makes BackTo identical whether native or synthesized, which the VM binding checks by running every case on both capabilities. The stand-in Flutter router shows the suppression is small.

decisions.question: Does the executor write the router's initial route at construction, and does it report a construction after start()?

options.label: write the initial top to nav.current-route (no history entry) and report LateExecutorConstruction in dev mode
options.consequence: nav.current-route is truthful from start(); the bootstrap mistake that loses a queued deep link is visible

options.label: leave RouteState.initial until the first navigation, no diagnostic
options.consequence: less code; nav.current-route reads NavRoute.none until the user navigates

decisions.chosen: write the initial top to nav.current-route (no history entry) and report LateExecutorConstruction in dev mode
decisions.why: Guide §3.5 makes construction before start() part of the bootstrap order; bus-api@v1's LateApplicationActivation is the analogous runtime diagnostic. No history entry because no transition was confirmed.

decisions.question: Whether this contract declares the in-memory router publicly, and where its binding lives.

options.label: public InMemoryRouter in package:nidana_dart_navigation/testing.dart; its binding in this contract's fixture directory
options.consequence: apps and nidana.integration get a VM router for navigation tests without Flutter; ADR-001 item 4 puts the binding here because this Interface declares it

options.label: a private stand-in inside the fixtures only
options.consequence: no public test double; every consumer writes its own, each needing its own binding (ADR-001 item 11)

options.label: in the main library
options.consequence: test infrastructure in the production import

decisions.chosen: public InMemoryRouter in package:nidana_dart_navigation/testing.dart; its binding in this contract's fixture directory
decisions.why: Mirrors the runtime's testing.dart (ADR-002 item 3: other public libraries named by their contract); nidana.navigation's isolation strategy already names an in-memory router; G26 keeps testing.dart free of test and flutter_test imports.

decisions.question: How are the conformance cases split between libraries and bindings?

options.label: two libraries: a VM-only navigation suite on TestBus (one implementation) and a runner-neutral executor suite (one per platform), the VM binding registering each executor case on both pop-until capabilities
options.consequence: resolver cases can assert with TestBus, stub, input and recorder literals; the executor harness names no bus-testing type; synthesized BackTo runs end to end on the VM

options.label: one library with a harness abstracting the bus for everything
options.consequence: resolver cases lose TestBus's deterministic recorder and must run under testWidgets too

decisions.chosen: two libraries: a VM-only navigation suite on TestBus (one implementation) and a runner-neutral executor suite (one per platform), the VM binding registering each executor case on both pop-until capabilities
decisions.why: bus-testing@v1's note: resolver tests run on a TestBus, while the executor harness must not name TestBus or settle; topology-dsl@v1's recording and live split is the precedent. The second registration keeps the guarantee-id prefix so --guarantee selects both (T8 in the experiment).

decisions.question: Is the app's deep-link mapping total or may it return nothing?

options.label: total: DeepLinkResolver returns a ResolvedNavIntent
options.consequence: every intent yields exactly one resolved intent; an unknown link maps to a route the app chooses

options.label: nullable: null drops the link
options.consequence: silent drops; one more filter stage in the template

decisions.chosen: total: DeepLinkResolver returns a ResolvedNavIntent
decisions.why: Keeps G14's one-to-one mapping and makes unknown links observable as navigations (Guide §3.1 'unobservable transitions'). Signal: an app that must ignore unknown links silently.

decisions.question: Does the contract pin the resolver template's stages and ids, and the access-requirement spelling?

options.label: pin id nav-resolver, APPLICATION scope, reads, writes and the stage order; requirement variants PublicAccess, AuthenticatedAccess, RoleAccess, CustomAccess with a fallback on the policy
options.consequence: the IR (Spec §6.5) shows resolve-before-guard and is checkable; equal configurations record equal definitions (idempotent activation); names do not collide with app ADT variants such as AuthState.Authenticated

options.label: pin only reads and writes; variants named Public, Authenticated, Role, Custom
options.consequence: freer implementation; the ordering fix is not visible in the IR; Authenticated collides with the Guide's own AuthState.Authenticated in an app that imports both

decisions.chosen: pin id nav-resolver, APPLICATION scope, reads, writes and the stage order; requirement variants PublicAccess, AuthenticatedAccess, RoleAccess, CustomAccess with a fallback on the policy
decisions.why: Guide §3.4 fixes the id and scope; pinning the stages makes Refinement 3 checkable from the recorded IR. The fallback lets an app close unlisted routes. No experiment for the variant collision beyond the Guide's naming.

decisions.question: How does the contract own result handling (Guide §3.6)?

options.label: a resultsFor helper over the topology DSL (withLatestFrom, filter, map) plus the stated pattern
options.consequence: the Guide's pattern once, recordable and testable; matching on payloads only

options.label: pattern only, no declaration
options.consequence: nothing to test; each app rewrites the three stages

decisions.chosen: a resultsFor helper over the topology DSL (withLatestFrom, filter, map) plus the stated pattern
decisions.why: nidana.navigation's Owns list includes result handling; a helper gives G16 a target. No evidence that apps need more.

decisions.question: Names and defaults: executor default name, resolver id, history buffer, testing library name.

options.label: ExecutorSource('navigation') by default; resolver id 'nav-resolver', not configurable; nav.history buffer 20; testing.dart
options.consequence: Guide §3.3 and §3.4 values; Flutter passes its own name such as 'flutter-navigation'; one resolver per bus

options.label: name required, id configurable
options.consequence: more ceremony at every construction; two resolvers on one bus would race on nav.resolved-intent anyway

decisions.chosen: ExecutorSource('navigation') by default; resolver id 'nav-resolver', not configurable; nav.history buffer 20; testing.dart
decisions.why: Guide values where it gives them; no evidence otherwise.

decisions.question: The S11 stand-in runtime delivers an activation's connection one microtask after activate, so a deep link queued before start() reaches the resolver's withLatestFrom before its auth read has a value and is dropped. Do the fixtures pin the real bootstrap (activate; start; with nothing between) or let microtasks run between activation and start()?

options.label: pin the real bootstrap and read bus-api@v1 G22 with G34 as requiring the connection before the queue (Refinement 8)
options.consequence: G14 and G24 fail against a runtime that does not deliver the connection first; bus-api@v1 needs its statement and fixtures sharpened; the experiment's runtime copy carries the change and still passes every bus-api@v1 and bus-testing@v1 case

options.label: flush between activation and start() in the cases
options.consequence: passes on the S11 stand-in, but tests a bootstrap no app writes (Guide §3.5 calls start() right after activation), so a real deep-link drop would pass the gate

decisions.chosen: pin the real bootstrap and read bus-api@v1 G22 with G34 as requiring the connection before the queue (Refinement 8)
decisions.why: Spec §3.13 and Guide §3.5 promise that a deep link published before start() is delivered once the resolver is subscribed; bus-api@v1 G22 already says the connection reaches reads before later values, but no bus-api case pins it and its G34 case flushes before start(). The probe shows the drop on the S11 runtime and the fix keeping bus-api's 86, 43 and bus-testing's 45 cases green. Under testWidgets the drop is hidden because pumpWidget runs the microtask before start().

decisions.question: bus-api@v1's publish<T>(MultiWriterTopic<T>, T) widens T, so publishing a DeepLink to nav.resolved-intent compiles. Does this contract carry a reject line for it now?

options.label: state G1 for this contract's own declarations and record the gap (Refinement 9)
options.consequence: every navigation-api fixture passes against bus-api@v1 as written; the publish hole is closed by an amendment of bus-api@v1, after which a reject line can be added here compatibly

options.label: add a reject line expecting could_not_infer now
options.consequence: the line fails until bus-api@v1 is amended, so nidana.navigation's gate would depend on another contract's pending change

decisions.chosen: state G1 for this contract's own declarations and record the gap (Refinement 9)
decisions.why: The probe shows W1 and W2 compile today and that the bounded form publish<T, V extends T> rejects both with could_not_infer while accepting well-typed publishes (W5); at run time the stand-in throws TypeError at delivery. The gap violates Spec §4.2 for every topic, so it belongs to bus-api@v1.

decisions.question: Seeded defects survived (from read off the bus, argsOf with a same-typed other route, query-parameter equality). Add cases or accept the gaps?

options.label: add the three assertions
options.consequence: G21 gains a case for confirmations made inside one delivery chain; G5 and G8 cases tighten

options.label: accept
options.consequence: an executor that reads from via getCurrentValue, and two equality defects, would pass the suite

decisions.chosen: add the three assertions
decisions.why: Each was a real defect the suite let through in the experiment's mutation runs.

experiments.question: Do the navigation-api@v1 fixtures hold against an implementation of the Interface: surface clean, reject codes exact, both suites passing, the executor suite binding under dart test and under testWidgets on a production-provider bus, and every suite case non-vacuous?
experiments.finding: Surface clean; all six reject files pass with confirmed codes (one pattern_never_matches_value_type warning); structure 27 guarantees, 66 cases, 2 bindings; navigation suite 40/40; executor suite 52/52 on InMemoryRouter (both capabilities) and 26/26 under fvm flutter test with testWidgets against a stand-in Flutter router over Navigator on a production-provider bus; 33 seeded defects each fail the cases of their guarantee.

experiments.question: When does an activation's connection reach its reads relative to a value published right after activate (bus-api@v1 G22) and to the queue start() delivers (G34)?
experiments.finding: On the S11 stand-in runtime one microtask later: a withLatestFrom over a state read drops a value published right after activate and a value queued before an immediate start(). With the connection made synchronous and its outputs deferred to a provider-zone microtask, both reach the read first, and bus-api@v1 (86 + 43) and bus-testing@v1 (45) cases still pass unchanged. On the S11 runtime the navigation suites fail exactly one G14 case and the G24 cases on the VM; under testWidgets pumpWidget hides it.

experiments.question: Does bus-api@v1's publish signature, or a generic intent constructor, check the value against the topic or route type?
experiments.finding: Neither: publish(NavigationTopics.resolvedIntent, DeepLink) and publish(EventTopic<int>, 'one') compile; GenericGoTo(route, 'one') compiles unless the context fixes the type. publish<T, V extends T> rejects both with could_not_infer and accepts well-typed calls; route.go('one') is argument_type_not_assignable. At run time the stand-in throws TypeError at delivery.

experiments.question: Which navigation-api names collide with what a Flutter page imports?
experiments.finding: Only the Specification's Route (ambiguous_import with package:flutter/widgets.dart); every declaration of this contract, testing.dart included, coexists with package:flutter/material.dart.

notes_for_orchestrator: OQ-N1 decided in navigation-api@v1 Refinement 2 and G13: navResolver<S> takes the app's StateTopic<S> and a pure AccessPrincipal Function(S); applyAuthGuard decides over the library's sealed AccessPrincipal (Pending, Anonymous, Authenticated with roles) with app-provided AccessRedirects. nidana.navigation's phase planning marks OQ-N1 RESOLVED pointing at navigation-api@v1.

OQ-N2 decided in navigation-api@v1 Refinement 1 and G2: typed NavRoute<A>; GoTo, Replace and ShowModal are built only by route.go/replace/showModal with an optional A? argument; RouteState.args is Object?, read typed through route.argsOf(state); path and query parameters stay Map<String, String>. nidana.navigation's phase planning marks OQ-N2 RESOLVED; OQ-F1's dependency on it is settled (the Flutter router passes the NavigationEntry, args included, through RouteSettings.arguments or its own table).

S13 (flutter-binding@v1) must: (1) declare a Flutter NavigationRouter (inside FlutterNavigationExecutor) meeting navigation-api@v1 G18: stack synchronous after perform, validate a whole perform before touching the Navigator (StateError, nothing done), apply PushRoute/ReplaceRoute/PopRoute/PopUntilRoute, confirm exactly once per perform with the resulting stack and the intent while suppressing its observer's pops during the perform, confirm a platform pop with const Back(), never pop the root on a system back; map GoTo to push (Refinement 7), not go_router's go; declare supportsPopUntil truthfully (Navigator.popUntil: true). (2) Bind hsdd/contract/fixture/navigation-api/behavior/navigation_executor_conformance.dart from hsdd/contract/fixture/flutter-binding/behavior/{implementation}_test.dart, importing it by the relative path ../../navigation-api/behavior/navigation_executor_conformance.dart, under testWidgets: bus() constructs Bus(config) in the body (production provider), executor() pumps the widget that hosts the router and then constructs NavigationExecutor(bus, router, name: name), platformBack() performs a system back (the stand-in uses navigatorKey.currentState!.maybePop(); tester.binding.handlePopRoute() is protected) then pumpAndSettle, elapse() is tester.pump(duration), settle() is tester.pumpAndSettle(), and the testWidgets body shuts every bus down and unmounts in a finally before it ends (ADR-003 item 7). A working template, 26/26 passing, is docs/auto-run/experiments/navigation-api-fixtures/standin_bindings/flutter_navigation_standin_test.dart with packages/flutter_navigation_standin/. (3) List that binding in flutter-binding@v1's Validation. (4) Settle the Flutter bootstrap: NavigationExecutor reads router.stack at construction, so either the Navigator is mounted before construction and start() runs after the first frame, or the router accepts calls before mount; G24 and LateExecutorConstruction assume construction before start(). (5) The module-scope RouteObserver can read NavRoute paths from the NavigationEntry the router puts in RouteSettings.arguments.

bus-api@v1 needs an amendment step (compatible statement sharpening plus fixtures; no consumer code exists yet): (a) G22/G34: state that the connection of a topology activated before start() reaches its reads before start() delivers the queue, while the publishes it causes wait for a provider-zone microtask, and add cases for both G22's 'published right after activate' clause and an activate-then-start bootstrap with no flush, for example a withLatestFrom gate over a state read (tool/connection_probe.dart). The S11 stand-in fails both; the experiment's patched copy (marked 'navigation-api-fixtures patch' in packages/nidana_dart_runtime/lib/src/interpreter.dart and bus.dart) shows a runtime can satisfy them while passing every existing bus-api@v1 and bus-testing@v1 case. nidana.runtime's design (OQ-R1 first delivery) must honour this. (b) Bus.publish and Publisher.publish should be publish<T, V extends T>(MultiWriterTopic<T> topic, V value) to meet Spec §4.2's compile-time typing; today publish(EventTopic<int>, 'one') and publish(NavigationTopics.resolvedIntent, DeepLink(uri)) compile (probe/widening.dart W1, W2). The type-parameter change breaks only callers that pass explicit type arguments. After (b), navigation-api@v1 can gain a compatible reject line for G1 on nav.resolved-intent.

Upstream items (would_upstream): Spec Appendix A.6 and Guide §3.2 name the route type Route, which collides with Flutter's Route; Guide §3.4 guards before resolving deep links, which lets a deep link bypass the guard; the Specification does not give intents stack semantics, and Guide §3.4 maps GoTo to go_router's location-based go.

Sweep for nidana.navigation's planning or reconcile: its spec's Owns list names `Route`; the contract's name is `NavRoute` (Refinement 5). Its isolation strategy (in-memory router, no Flutter) matches InMemoryRouter in testing.dart.
nidana.integration's guarded-navigation and bootstrap slices rest on Refinement 8; its gate (--all) will run both navigation bindings and flutter-binding@v1's binding of the executor suite.
